topic: Frontier Lab · Phase 4: Kernels, Quantization & Decoding

questions.title: Pallas vs XLA — when to hand-write a kernel
questions.prompt: XLA already fuses and compiles your JAX ops. When would you drop down to a hand-written Pallas kernel instead, and what does that actually buy you?
probes: What control does Pallas give you over memory that XLA's fusion decisions don't?
What's the engineering cost of going this route?
criteria: XLA auto-fusion limits
explicit memory hierarchy control
block/grid specification
when the win is real (memory-bound ops)
cost: portability, dev time, debugging

no_hire.answer: Pallas is a lower-level way to write GPU code that's faster than XLA.
no_hire.interviewer_note: No mechanism, no concrete scenario, no cost side.

weak_hire.answer: XLA compiles a fixed fusion strategy for your ops, so if the op is unusual it may not fuse optimally. Pallas lets you write a custom kernel to control exactly how memory is moved between HBM and on-chip memory, which helps for memory-bound ops like attention. The cost is you have to write and debug low-level code yourself.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Right shape and right example, but no concrete grid/block mechanism and no worked failure example of XLA falling short.

hire.answer: XLA's fusion is a compiler heuristic: it decides tiling and buffer placement for you, which works well for standard patterns but can leave memory-bound kernels (attention, custom normalization, sparse gather/scatter) reading/writing HBM more than necessary because it won't restructure the algorithm, only fuse ops. Pallas lets you explicitly define the grid (how the problem is partitioned across invocations) and block specs (what tile of each tensor is loaded into VMEM/SRAM per grid step), so you control the exact memory access pattern — e.g. keeping a whole K/V tile resident in fast memory across a loop instead of round-tripping through HBM. You pay for it in portability (kernel is TPU- or GPU-specific), dev/debug time, and losing XLA's automatic gradient/fusion for that region.
hire.interviewer_note: Names grid/block specs and VMEM residency concretely, and states the real cost. Solid hire.

strong_hire.answer: XLA fuses within its cost model but treats each op's data-movement as fixed by the op's mathematical definition; it can't rewrite an algorithm to change what needs to touch HBM at all. Pallas kernels let you co-design the algorithm and the memory layout — the canonical case is FlashAttention: rewriting softmax with an online/running formulation specifically so you never materialize the N x N score matrix, which is an algorithmic change XLA's fusion pass would never make on its own, only Pallas/CUDA-level control lets you express it. In practice you reach for Pallas when profiling shows a kernel is memory-bandwidth-bound and the arithmetic intensity could be raised by restructuring tiling (grid/block spec, VMEM/SRAM residency, double-buffering across grid steps) — not for compute-bound matmuls where XLA/cuBLAS already saturate the tensor cores. The cost is real: you lose XLA's automatic differentiation and cross-op fusion for that region (often need a hand-written backward pass too), the kernel is hardware-specific and needs re-tuning per chip generation (block sizes, VMEM budget), and it multiplies your test/debug surface. I'd only invest here after a roofline/profiler shows the theoretical ceiling is meaningfully above what XLA achieves.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Names the algorithmic-rewrite distinction (not just faster fusion), ties to FlashAttention as the motivating case, gives the profiling-first decision rule and the full cost list including backward-pass burden. Staff-level.

questions.title: FlashAttention IO-awareness and exactness
questions.prompt: Explain how FlashAttention computes exact softmax attention without ever materializing the full N x N attention matrix in HBM, and quantify the HBM traffic improvement.
probes: How does the online softmax keep a running max and sum without seeing all scores at once?
Why is this mathematically exact and not an approximation?
criteria: tiling Q/K/V into SRAM-sized blocks
online softmax with running max and running sum
never writes N x N to HBM
exact, not approximate
HBM traffic O(N^2) -> ~O(N^2/M) reduction

no_hire.answer: FlashAttention is a faster version of attention that uses less memory by approximating the softmax.
no_hire.interviewer_note: Wrong on exactness — it's exact, not approximate. No mechanism at all.

weak_hire.answer: Normally you compute all of QK^T, store the N x N matrix, softmax it, then multiply by V — that N x N matrix is huge and slow to read/write. FlashAttention processes the sequence in blocks so it never has to store the whole matrix, using a technique that updates the softmax incrementally as it sees each block.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Right high-level picture and correctly avoids calling it approximate, but 'updates the softmax incrementally' is hand-wavy — no running max/sum mechanism, no traffic numbers.

hire.answer: Standard attention writes the N x N score matrix to HBM to do a global softmax over each row, which for long N is what actually dominates runtime — it's memory-bound, not compute-bound. FlashAttention tiles Q, K, V into blocks sized to fit in SRAM, and for each Q block loops over K/V blocks, maintaining a running max m and running sum of exponentials l for the softmax normalization; each time a new K/V block arrives it rescales the accumulated output by exp(m_old - m_new) and folds in the new contribution — this is the online softmax trick, and it's exact because it's just an algebraic reassociation of the same softmax sum, no terms dropped. The N x N matrix is never written to HBM, only read once from Q/K/V and written once for O, cutting HBM traffic from O(N^2) to roughly O(N^2/M) where M is SRAM block size.
hire.interviewer_note: Correct mechanism (running max/sum, rescaling), states exactness reason, and gives the traffic bound. Strong hire.

strong_hire.answer: The key insight is that attention is memory-bound: computing QK^T, softmax, and the second matmul is cheap in FLOPs relative to the HBM round-trips of writing and re-reading the N x N intermediate, so the fix is an IO-aware algorithm, not a faster matmul. FlashAttention uses tiling: partition Q into blocks of size B_r and K/V into blocks of size B_c that fit in on-chip SRAM (~192KB on A100), and for each Q block iterate over K/V blocks in an inner loop, computing partial scores S_ij = Q_i K_j^T in SRAM. Online softmax keeps two running statistics per row — the running max m_i and running sum of exp(s - m_i) — and on seeing a new block, updates m_i^new = max(m_i^old, rowmax(S_ij)), rescales the previous accumulator by exp(m_i^old - m_i^new), and adds the new block's contribution exp(S_ij - m_i^new) V_j; this is exact because softmax(x) = exp(x-max)/sum(exp(x-max)) is invariant to which max you subtract as long as you correct consistently, so incremental max updates with rescaling reproduce the exact same normalized output as a one-shot global softmax — no approximation, just reassociating the sum. HBM traffic: naive attention is Theta(N*d + N^2) reads/writes (dominated by the N^2 term for the score matrix and its softmax pass); FlashAttention is Theta(N^2 * d^2 / M) where M is SRAM size, which for typical M >> d gives a reduction roughly proportional to block size, and critically it never touches HBM with an N x N tensor — only O(Nd) traffic for Q/K/V/O plus the tiled recomputation, which also lets the backward pass avoid storing the N x N matrix by recomputing it from stored (m, l) statistics rather than checkpointing it, trading FLOPs (cheap, compute-bound) for HBM traffic (expensive, memory-bound).
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Gives the block-size dependent traffic formula, explains the rescale-and-correct exactness argument precisely, and extends to the backward pass recomputation tradeoff — the compute-for-memory trade is the deepest part interviewers look for. Principal-level.

questions.title: SRAM bank conflicts, tiling, and FA2/FA3 hardware evolution
questions.prompt: Beyond the online-softmax algorithm, what low-level GPU details (shared memory layout, warp scheduling) determine whether a kernel like FlashAttention actually hits peak throughput, and how did FlashAttention-2/3 change to exploit newer hardware?
probes: What is a shared-memory bank conflict and how does tiling/padding avoid it?
What did Hopper's async copy and TMA change about how you write these kernels?
criteria: shared memory banked into 32 banks, conflict = multiple threads same bank
tile/pad layout to stride across banks
FA2: better work partitioning, fewer non-matmul ops, parallelize over sequence too
FA3: warp specialization + Hopper async/TMA overlap
occupancy vs register/shared-mem pressure tradeoff

no_hire.answer: FlashAttention 2 and 3 are just faster reimplementations with better code.
no_hire.interviewer_note: No specifics on why they're faster — no bank conflicts, no warp specialization, no hardware feature named.

weak_hire.answer: Shared memory is split into banks and if multiple threads hit the same bank at once you get a slowdown, so kernels lay out data to spread accesses across banks. FlashAttention-2 improved GPU utilization by better parallelizing the work across thread blocks, and FlashAttention-3 added support for newer Hopper GPU features to go even faster.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Correctly names bank conflicts and gestures at FA2/FA3 improvements, but no mechanism for how work is repartitioned or what the Hopper features actually are (async copy, TMA, warp specialization).

hire.answer: GPU shared memory is organized into 32 banks; if multiple threads in a warp access different addresses that map to the same bank in the same cycle, accesses serialize instead of running in parallel — a bank conflict. Kernels avoid this by padding tile strides so consecutive threads land in different banks. FlashAttention-1 parallelized mainly over batch and heads, leaving the sequence dimension underutilized for long sequences with few heads; FlashAttention-2 restructured the loop order to also parallelize over the sequence/query-block dimension and reduced non-matmul FLOPs (fewer rescaling ops relative to matmul ops), better matching GPU occupancy. FlashAttention-3 targets Hopper specifically: it uses warp specialization, where separate warps are dedicated to loading data (via async copy) versus doing the matmul compute, so data movement and compute overlap instead of serializing.
hire.interviewer_note: Correct bank-conflict mechanism, correct FA2 parallelization change, and names warp specialization for FA3. Strong.

strong_hire.answer: Shared memory has 32 banks addressed by (address / 4 bytes) mod 32 for 32-bit words; a conflict occurs when >1 thread in a warp accesses different addresses in the same bank in one cycle, forcing serialized replay — the classic fix is padding a tile's row stride by one extra element so that a column-major or transposed access pattern doesn't line up every thread on the same bank, at the cost of a little wasted shared memory. FlashAttention-2's changes were about work partitioning, not the algorithm: FA1 parallelized the grid over (batch, head), which starves the GPU of parallelism for long-context/few-head/small-batch regimes since block count is too low to fill all SMs; FA2 additionally splits along the query sequence dimension so block count scales with sequence length, and it swaps loop order so the outer loop is over K/V blocks and inner over Q blocks in the backward pass to cut redundant shared-memory traffic, plus reduces the fraction of non-matmul FLOPs (rescaling, bookkeeping) since those don't use tensor cores and become the bottleneck once matmul is fast. FlashAttention-3 is built around Hopper's specific primitives: warp-specialized producer/consumer roles where dedicated 'producer' warps issue asynchronous TMA (Tensor Memory Accelerator) copies moving tiles from HBM/global memory directly into shared memory without occupying compute warps, while 'consumer' warps run the WGMMA (warp-group matrix multiply) instructions on tensor cores — this overlaps the async data movement with compute across pipeline stages instead of the load-then-compute serialization FA2 had, and FA3 also exploits FP8 with incoherent processing to reduce quantization error for the matmuls. The general tension across all of this is occupancy versus resource pressure: bigger tiles reduce HBM traffic and non-matmul overhead but increase shared-memory and register usage per thread block, which caps how many blocks can be resident per SM simultaneously — tuning block size is a search over this occupancy/traffic tradeoff, and it's why FA kernels ship different tile configs per GPU architecture.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Gives the exact bank-conflict formula, names TMA and WGMMA specifically with producer/consumer warp roles, and closes with the occupancy-vs-resource-pressure tradeoff that governs all tile-size tuning. Systems-level mastery.

questions.title: LLM.int8 outliers and QuIP/QuIP# incoherence for 2-bit
questions.prompt: Explain why activation outliers force LLM.int8() into mixed precision, then explain how QuIP/QuIP# use incoherence processing to push weight quantization down to 2 bits where naive methods fail badly.
probes: Why can't you just clip or rescale the outlier channels away?
What does a random orthogonal (Hadamard) rotation actually change about the weight distribution?
criteria: outlier features concentrated in few channels, systematic not random
mixed-precision decomposition: outliers in FP16, rest in INT8
incoherence = no single weight/direction dominates after rotation
Hadamard/random orthogonal transform spreads magnitude
why this enables far more aggressive (2-bit) quantization

no_hire.answer: Outliers are just large weight values that mess up quantization, so LLM.int8 keeps them in higher precision.
no_hire.interviewer_note: Confuses activation outliers with weight outliers, and gives no mechanism for QuIP at all.

weak_hire.answer: In large models, a few activation dimensions have much larger magnitude than the rest, and if you quantize those the same way as everything else you get big errors that hurt output quality. LLM.int8 keeps those outlier dimensions in FP16 and quantizes the rest in INT8. QuIP uses a mathematical transformation to spread out the weight values before quantizing so they're more uniform, which lets you go to very low bit counts like 2-bit.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Correct high-level picture for both methods, but 'mathematical transformation to spread out values' doesn't name incoherence or the Hadamard/orthogonal mechanism, and no explanation of why outliers are structural rather than random.

hire.answer: Activation outliers in large transformers are systematic: they emerge in specific feature dimensions (often correlated with a few attention heads or layers) with magnitude 10-100x the rest, and because quantization error scales with the range you're forced to cover, a handful of huge values blow up the quantization scale for every other value in that tensor. LLM.int8() decomposes the matmul: outlier columns (identified by activation magnitude) are computed in FP16, the rest in INT8 with per-row/column scaling, avoiding the shared-scale problem. QuIP's incoherence processing multiplies weights (and activations) by random orthogonal matrices (efficiently realized via Hadamard transforms) before quantization; this spreads any large or structured values across all coordinates so no single weight or direction dominates the quantization error, which is what lets round-to-nearest work well even at 2 bits — you invert the rotation after dequantization since orthogonal transforms are invertible and don't change the matmul's mathematical result.
hire.interviewer_note: Correctly explains why outliers break shared-scale quantization, the mixed-precision fix, and the incoherence mechanism with invertibility. Strong hire.

strong_hire.answer: The outlier phenomenon (Dettmers et al.) is emergent above ~6B parameters: a small number of feature dimensions develop systematically large activations across almost all tokens, and because a single quantization scale must cover the full range of a tensor, these outliers force the scale so wide that the remaining ~99% of normal-magnitude values get crushed into a handful of INT8 levels, destroying their signal — clipping loses information outright and per-tensor rescaling can't fix a problem that's concentrated in specific columns, not the whole distribution. LLM.int8() decomposes the matmul into two parts along the outlier feature dimension: outlier columns (chosen by a fixed magnitude threshold, typically a small fixed count) go through in FP16 matmul, everything else goes through vectorized INT8 with per-row weight scales and per-column activation scales, recombined by addition — asymptotically cheap since outlier columns are a tiny fraction of dimensions. QuIP's incoherence processing addresses a different pathology: even without outliers, if quantization error correlates with specific weight directions (incoherent = error is unstructured/spread, coherent = a few directions carry disproportionate importance or magnitude), naive rounding at 2 bits accumulates catastrophic error along those directions. QuIP applies U^T W V where U, V are random orthogonal matrices (implemented efficiently as randomized Hadamard transforms in O(n log n) rather than dense O(n^2) matmuls) before rounding, which provably bounds the maximum entry magnitude and decorrelates the rounding error from any weight direction — formally, incoherence processing guarantees quantization error behaves like unstructured noise rather than a structured, correlated error that compounds through subsequent layers. QuIP# additionally replaces scalar round-to-nearest with a vector quantization codebook (E8 lattice-based) after incoherence processing, since incoherent (near-Gaussian, isotropic) vectors are exactly what lattice codebooks quantize efficiently, closing most of the remaining gap to 2-bit-competitive perplexity. The throughline across LLM.int8 and QuIP is the same: naive uniform quantization only works when error is unstructured and bounded; when structure exists (outlier channels, or correlated rounding directions), you either isolate the structure (mixed precision) or destroy it before quantizing (incoherence rotation) — production mitigation is to pick per-layer based on measured activation kurtosis/outlier count, since attention-output and down-projection layers often need different treatment than embeddings.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Explains the emergent-outlier phenomenon precisely, why per-tensor scaling structurally fails, the exact QuIP transform with efficient Hadamard implementation, ties to QuIP#'s lattice codebook rationale, and unifies both methods under a single 'destroy or isolate structured error' framework with a production decision heuristic. Research-lead depth.

questions.title: KV-cache decoding: SnapKV eviction and GQA/MQA head sharing
questions.prompt: Two different levers reduce KV-cache memory at decode time: SnapKV-style eviction and GQA/MQA head sharing. Explain how each works and the quality/memory trade each makes.
probes: How does SnapKV decide which tokens to evict without hurting quality?
Why does sharing K/V heads across query heads save memory, and what quality risk does it carry?
criteria: KV cache grows linearly with context, dominates decode memory
SnapKV: use attention patterns from an observation window to score and keep important tokens, evict the rest
GQA: groups of query heads share one K/V head; MQA: all query heads share one K/V head
memory savings scale with number of shared groups
quality tradeoff: eviction risks losing tokens needed later; head sharing risks losing head-specific representational capacity

no_hire.answer: You can just delete old tokens from the KV cache to save memory, and use fewer attention heads to make it smaller.
no_hire.interviewer_note: No selection mechanism for eviction, and 'fewer heads' confuses reducing query heads with sharing K/V heads — misses the actual GQA/MQA mechanism.

weak_hire.answer: SnapKV looks at which tokens the model has been attending to and keeps only the important ones, evicting the rest to save memory, which works because attention is sparse — most tokens don't matter much. GQA and MQA save memory by having multiple query heads share the same key/value heads instead of every head having its own, which shrinks the KV cache proportionally. The risk is losing information you evicted or needed a head to specialize on.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Correct general idea for both, but no concrete scoring mechanism for SnapKV and no quantification of the GQA/MQA memory reduction or where the sharing sits on the MQA-GQA-MHA spectrum.

hire.answer: KV cache size scales as 2 * layers * heads * head_dim * seq_len * batch, so at long context it dominates memory and caps batch size/throughput. SnapKV observes attention patterns over a recent window of the prompt (not the full generation) to identify which prior tokens consistently receive high attention weight across heads, clusters/pools these into important positions, and keeps only those plus a local recent window, evicting the rest before generation starts — this exploits the empirical finding that important tokens are consistent across generation steps, so a one-time compression barely hurts quality if the observation window is representative. GQA groups query heads into G groups, each group sharing one K/V head pair (G < number of query heads), reducing KV cache by a factor of num_heads/G; MQA is the extreme case G=1, all query heads share a single K/V head, maximizing memory savings but risking the most representational bottleneck since all heads must agree on what to attend to. The trade is memory/bandwidth savings versus quality: SnapKV risks evicting a token that becomes relevant later in generation (query-dependent importance that the observation window didn't capture); GQA/MQA risks losing head-specialization since heads that previously attended differently now share the same keys/values, usually recovered by training with grouping from scratch or short fine-tuning rather than post-hoc converting a trained MHA model.
hire.interviewer_note: Correct KV-size formula, correct SnapKV window/pooling mechanism, correct GQA/MQA spectrum with G, and states both failure risks. Strong hire.

strong_hire.answer: KV cache memory is 2 * L * H * d_h * S * B * bytes_per_element and at long context (S in the tens of thousands) it dwarfs weight memory, which is why both eviction and head-sharing exist as complementary, stackable levers rather than competitors. SnapKV's mechanism: during prefill, use the last portion of the prompt as an 'observation window' and compute attention scores from that window's queries against all prior keys; pool these scores (typically max or average pooling across a small kernel to avoid picking isolated high-attention tokens that are positionally accidental) and select the top-scoring positions as the 'important' clusters to retain, concatenated with a fixed recent-token window, then physically compress the cache to only those positions before decoding begins — this works because attention importance during generation is highly consistent with the importance pattern already visible near the end of the prompt (empirically validated per-head, since different heads attend to different structures like retrieval heads vs local heads), but it degrades on tasks where a needle only becomes relevant far into generation and wasn't attended to during the observation window, i.e. it trades a one-time, prompt-time compression decision for a risk of under-provisioning for future queries — production systems mitigate by keeping a generous budget and combining with a rolling/recent window as a safety net. GQA sits on a continuum between MHA (G = H, no sharing, best quality, largest cache) and MQA (G=1, maximal compression, historically the largest quality hit since a single K/V head must serve all query heads' different attention patterns); GQA's empirical sweet spot (Ainslie et al., used in Llama 2/3, Mistral) is G in the 4-8 range, recovering nearly all MHA quality at a fraction of the cache — the mechanism works because query heads within a group can still specialize in how they weight the shared keys/values (the query projections differ per head even though K/V are shared), so representational loss is smaller than naively expected. In production you stack these: GQA/MQA sets the architectural memory floor at training time (irreversible without retraining), and SnapKV/eviction operates on top at inference time as an orthogonal, model-agnostic compression layer — the joint decision is: pick G to hit a memory/quality target during pretraining, then use eviction policies to handle context lengths beyond what even the reduced cache can hold cheaply, monitoring needle-in-haystack-style recall regressions as the canary for over-aggressive eviction.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Gives the exact KV-size formula, the pooling detail in SnapKV eviction scoring, the retrieval-head vs local-head nuance, the MHA-GQA-MQA continuum with why per-head query specialization survives sharing, and closes with the production stacking strategy and the canary metric. Staff/principal depth.

questions.title: Speculative decoding acceptance math
questions.prompt: In speculative decoding, a draft model proposes k tokens and the target verifies them in one parallel pass. Explain the accept/reject rule that keeps the output distribution exact, and derive the expected number of accepted tokens as a function of acceptance probability alpha and k.
probes: Why is the acceptance rule provably exact rather than an approximation?
What happens to expected speedup as k grows for a fixed alpha?
criteria: accept token i with prob min(1, p_target/p_draft)
on reject, resample from normalized (p_target - p_draft)_+
distribution is exactly p_target, not approximate
expected accepted tokens = (1 - alpha^(k+1)) / (1 - alpha)
diminishing returns / cost tradeoff as k grows

no_hire.answer: The draft proposes k tokens and you accept the ones the target model agrees with, then just move on to generate the next batch.
no_hire.interviewer_note: No accept/reject probability rule, no exactness argument, no formula.

weak_hire.answer: For each proposed token you compare the draft's probability and the target's probability and accept it with some probability based on how much they agree; if rejected you sample a new token from the target instead. This keeps things roughly correct because the target has the final say. On average, if each token has acceptance probability alpha, you'd expect about alpha*k tokens accepted per round.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Gets the qualitative accept/reject idea and attempts a formula, but 'roughly correct' is wrong — it's exact, not approximate — and alpha*k is not the correct expectation (ignores the sequential dependency and the free resampled token).

hire.answer: For each position i, accept the draft's token with probability min(1, p_target(i)/p_draft(i)); if accepted, move to position i+1 using the same draft distribution context. If rejected, discard it and resample a token from the residual distribution normalized(max(0, p_target - p_draft)), then stop the block there. This is exact rejection sampling: the marginal distribution of the token you end up emitting at each position, integrated over accept and reject cases, is exactly p_target, not an approximation of it. If each position independently has acceptance probability alpha, the expected number of accepted tokens before the first rejection follows a geometric-like process, and the expected total tokens produced per round (accepted tokens plus the one guaranteed resampled/bonus token) is (1 - alpha^(k+1)) / (1 - alpha).
hire.interviewer_note: Correct rule, correct exactness statement, and states the right closed-form expectation. Strong hire.

strong_hire.answer: The accept/reject rule is standard rejection sampling adapted to two known distributions: accept token x_i ~ q (draft) with probability min(1, p(x_i)/q(x_i)) where p is the target distribution; conditioning on rejection, the residual distribution norm(max(0, p - q)) is exactly what's needed to make the process at position i marginally distributed as p — this is provable by direct calculation: P(emit x) = q(x)*min(1,p(x)/q(x)) + P(reject)*norm(max(0,p-q))(x), and expanding both cases algebraically collapses to p(x) for every x, with no approximation error regardless of how different p and q are (bad draft models just lower acceptance rate, they never bias the output). For the expectation: let alpha be the (assumed constant, i.i.d. for simplicity) per-token acceptance probability; the number of accepted tokens before the first rejection is geometric, and since you always get exactly one additional token from the resample-on-reject (or from continuing to draft if all k are accepted, effectively also 'free' relative to a second target pass), the expected number of tokens emitted per target verification pass is E[tokens] = sum_{i=0}^{k} alpha^i = (1 - alpha^(k+1)) / (1 - alpha), which as k -> infinity approaches 1/(1-alpha) — meaning there's a hard ceiling on expected tokens/pass set purely by alpha, and increasing k beyond that ceiling buys diminishing returns while linearly increasing wasted draft compute on the rejected tail. The real wall-clock speedup is this expected-tokens value divided by (1 + c) where c is the draft model's cost relative to one target forward pass, so the design problem is jointly choosing a draft model (to raise alpha, e.g. via distillation from the target, or self-speculation methods like Medusa/EAGLE that raise agreement by construction) and k (tuned near where the marginal accepted-token gain stops exceeding the marginal wasted draft FLOPs) — and note alpha itself is not really constant, it degrades with higher sampling temperature and with domains where the draft and target diverge (long-tail reasoning), so k should be tuned adaptively rather than fixed.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Full derivation of exactness via the rejection-sampling identity, the correct geometric-series closed form with its 1/(1-alpha) asymptotic ceiling, the joint draft-model/k design problem, and the adaptive-alpha caveat. Research-engineer depth.
